account: The Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) operates Alice, a text-mining robot. It reads federal tender notices and electronic-auction records daily and sends auditors a list of possible irregularities. Trade press in 2017 and 2018 expanded the name as “Análise de Licitações e Editais”. The TCU's own July 2020 release calls the tool the “Sistema de Análise de Licitações e Contratos (Alice)”. Trade press in September 2017 quoted TCU auditor Valéria Nakano as saying that Alice found two DNIT notices worth R$39 million. They were for maintaining stretches of BR-153 already under concession, and a TCU ruling (acórdão) blocked them within two months. That ruling is not available, so the example is unverified. In its 4 March 2022 statement on the benefits of its control work in 2021, the TCU reported the value captured through Alice. It was R$426 million in 2021 against R$194 million in 2020. Fernanda Odilla of the University of Bologna published an independent study of Brazilian anti-corruption bots in March 2023. She reports that the Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU) created Alice in 2015 before sharing it with the TCU. She also reports that Alice helped auditors stop irregular tenders and that its accuracy fell from 88.27% in testing to 73.91% in later auditing. She adds that auditors complained of inboxes overloaded with alerts that the TCU lacked staff to check. A TCU plenary ruling of 6 May 2026 records that the tool, now called Alice 360, has moved to intensive use of AI.

ai_role.statement: The TCU attributes the 2021 figure to control actions supported by Alice under its benefit-measurement method. It says “o segundo de fato reflete o benefício calculado, que resultou da ação de controle e foi medido”. No independent evaluation or counterfactual was found. The 2017 DNIT/BR-153 example rests on a trade-press interview with a TCU auditor. The TCU acórdão was not available. Developer and deployer are the same public body.

evidence.citation: Fernanda Odilla, Bots against corruption: Exploring the benefits and limitations of AI-based anti-corruption technology, Crime, Law and Social Change 80(4): 353-396, 25 March 2023. The author worked at the University of Bologna with no stake in the TCU or the CGU; her study draws on desk research, access-to-information requests and interviews with developers. She reports that Alice has helped auditors stop irregular tenders and that its accuracy fell from 88.27% in testing to 73.91% in later auditing, without separating its use at the CGU from its use at the TCU.

fields.account: The Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) operates Alice, a text-mining robot. It reads federal tender notices and electronic-auction records daily and sends auditors a list of possible irregularities. Trade press in 2017 and 2018 expanded the name as “Análise de Licitações e Editais”. The TCU's own July 2020 release calls the tool the “Sistema de Análise de Licitações e Contratos (Alice)”. Trade press in September 2017 quoted TCU auditor Valéria Nakano as saying that Alice found two DNIT notices worth R$39 million. They were for maintaining stretches of BR-153 already under concession, and a TCU ruling (acórdão) blocked them within two months. That ruling is not available, so the example is unverified. In its 4 March 2022 statement on the benefits of its control work in 2021, the TCU reported the value captured through Alice. It was R$426 million in 2021 against R$194 million in 2020. Fernanda Odilla of the University of Bologna published an independent study of Brazilian anti-corruption bots in March 2023. She reports that the Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU) created Alice in 2015 before sharing it with the TCU. She also reports that Alice helped auditors stop irregular tenders and that its accuracy fell from 88.27% in testing to 73.91% in later auditing. She adds that auditors complained of inboxes overloaded with alerts that the TCU lacked staff to check. A TCU plenary ruling of 6 May 2026 records that the tool, now called Alice 360, has moved to intensive use of AI.
